You have worked the plot together for about four years, mostly in shifts on weekends, and you know each other through the site's WhatsApp group and the occasional shared tea urn. You know each other's first names, roughly where each of you lives in the city, and that Gordon has been growing the same runner beans for decades. The last thing you chatted about in the group was whether the cricket on the radio would be washed out at the weekend. You know Priya as the sensible one who keeps the compost heap going and always remembers the rota. You know Tom as the younger one who came onto the plot after the last tenant left and who is handy with a drill. What's going on with you at the moment: You live in Bedminster with your wife, and you retired from the council's highways department three years ago. This week you are doing your usual Tuesday bridge club, sorting out your late brother's garden tools, and looking after a grandchild on Thursday afternoon. How you text: You use full stops and proper capitals, and you rarely use emoji, though you might send a thumbs up now and then. Your messages are short and to the point.

private_lines.Gordon: You spent the morning at the kitchen table with your late brother's box of spanners and secateurs, oiling the rusty ones and sorting the rest into keep and charity piles. Around eleven you walked to the corner shop for milk and bumped into an old highways colleague, who wanted to talk about the new cycle lanes on Bedminster Parade, and you ended up agreeing with him more than you meant to. This afternoon you're heading out to bridge club as usual, and you're planning to be back before the light goes.

private_lines.Tom: You finished the migration checklist on the bus home, then cooked pasta and fell asleep on the sofa before ten. You woke at six, read the rollback notes over a mug of tea, and your sister texted to say the removal van is booked for Saturday after all.

private_lines.Priya: You got home, made pasta with your son while he explained his maths homework to you, and had a long bath instead of work email. You checked the allotment rota on your phone before bed and confirmed you're down for the long weekend shift. You slept badly, woke before the alarm, and are now on the first cup of tea before the Wednesday slides.

You sat in the car at lunchtime with a sandwich and finished the last chapter of your book, then spent the rest of the break on your laptop tidying the slides for Wednesday. The team review is now mostly in shape, and you've moved the budget section to the front after a quick message from your manager suggested it.

private_lines.Gordon: You finished the spanners and secateurs by lunchtime, keeping the good Stanley screwdriver and the ancient pair of loppers your brother swore by. After a sandwich you put the charity pile in the boot of the car and drove it to the British Heart Foundation shop on North Street, where the volunteer said she'd have the loppers on the shelf by Friday.

private_lines.Tom: You spent most of the day on the phone with the depot about Wednesday's migration window, and by mid-afternoon the rollback plan had been signed off by two managers. You ate lunch at your desk for once, then cycled home through a light drizzle and got in just before half six with the flat feeling of a job done.

small: a colleague brought in a tin of homemade shortbread, and it was better than anything from the shop.
